newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada accuses U.S. of breaching salmon treaty.
newsitem.headline: Canada accuses U.S. of breaching salmon treaty.

text.p: Canada fired off a terse "diplomatic note" to the United States on Friday, accusing it of breaching an international treaty by overfishing in Alaska.

"We're basically saying they're violating a treaty. It's a very serious matter," Foreign Affairs Minister Lloyd Axworthy told a news conference. "In effect, what we're saying is, 'You've already caught more than you deserve. You should stop catching it.'"

The diplomatic note accuses the United States of failing to live up to its obligations under the 1985 Pacific salmon treaty and takes the dispute between the two countries over salmon fishing to a more intense level, Axworthy said.
He added that he expected to hear from (U.S.) Secretary of State Madeleine Albright by next week on the matter.
Alaskan fishermen have been catching a high level of Canada-bound sockeye salmon, Canada's Fisheries Minister David Anderson said at the news conference.

He estimated that Alaskans had caught C$1.9 million ($1.4 million) worth of sockeye salmon or about 350,000 fish so far in the 1997 season -- an increase of 300 percent from the average of previous years.

"This is inconsistent with past practices for this period and represents a record catch for this time of year," the Canadian government said in its diplomatic note. "The increase in sockeye interceptions is not justified."
Canada has asked the U.S. government to intervene to make sure the treaty is respected.
Axworthy recognized, however, that the treaty provided for no sanctions.
Canada and the United States have been negotiating sporadically for months to try to settle the dispute and agree on catch levels within the framework of the treaty.
